kzz7yh-a78315-d1e103.summary: Announces that four questions are raised about the first topic of the distinction, God's existence in things.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e108.summary: Lists the first two questions: whether God is in all things by essence, presence and power, and whether he is in all things equally.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e115.summary: Lists the third question: whether being everywhere belongs to God alone.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e120.summary: Lists the fourth question: whether God is outside every place.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e130.summary: First objection: Anselm (Monologion 22) says God is more fittingly said to be with place and time than in them, and properly in no place; a place is a thing, so God is not in all things.
claims: God is properly in no place (objection).

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e146.summary: Second objection: John of Damascus says God, immutable and uncircumscribable, is not in place but is his own place; hence he is not in all things.
claims: God is his own place and not in place (objection).

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e155.summary: Third objection: a cause that can act both present and absent is nobler than one acting only when present; God, the noblest cause, can act in his absence, so he is not in all things by presence.
claims: The noblest cause can act at a distance (objection).

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e164.summary: Fourth objection: created causes give their effects a power of persisting by themselves; a fortiori God does, so he is not in all things by power.
claims: God gives creatures a power to persist by themselves (objection).

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e172.summary: Sed contra from Augustine's letter to Dardanus: God is everywhere by the presence of divinity, though not by the grace of indwelling; hence he is in all places and so in all things.
claims: God is everywhere by presence of divinity but not everywhere by indwelling grace.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e183.summary: Second sed contra: Gregory's gloss on the Song of Songs, cited by Lombard, says God is in all things in a common way by presence, power and substance.
claims: God is commonly in all things by presence, power and substance.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e190.summary: Third sed contra from Wisdom 8: uncreated wisdom reaches from end to end mightily and orders all things sweetly; so God is in all things.
claims: Divine wisdom reaches all things.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e197.summary: Richard's solution, first part: God is in all things, corporeal and spiritual, by essence, presence and power. By essence follows from his immensity, a positive infinity, and his supreme simplicity, so that he is whole in each thing. It also follows from the immediate emanation of all creatures from God, some immediately only and some immediately and through secondary causes too. Since essence and power are identical in God, whatever his power reaches his essence reaches.
claims: God is in all things by essence, presence and power.
God's essence is whole in each thing because of infinity and simplicity.
All creatures emanate immediately from God even when secondary causes are involved.
Because God's essence and power are identical, his essence is wherever his power acts.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e219.summary: God is in all things by presence through his omniscience: as things in a house are present to someone who sees them though he is not substantially in each part, so all things are present to God because they are in his sight.
claims: Presence means that all things are within God's view.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e232.summary: God is in all things by power, shown by his omnipotence and by creatures' weakness in being: they always need to be sustained, as Augustine (De Genesi ad litteram 4) and Avicenna say. The threefold mode refutes three errors: those who limit the divine essence or deny it is the immediate cause of being, those who deny God sees human affairs (Job 22), and the Manichees, who subject only spiritual things to God.
claims: Creatures need continual conservation by divine power.
God's presence by essence refutes a limited divine essence.
God's presence by power refutes Manichaean dualism.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e283.summary: Reply to the Anselm argument: Anselm denies that God is in place not because God is not present to place by essence, but because God is not contained by place, either circumscriptively or definitively, nor conserved by it; rather he conserves it. So God should not be called 'local'.
claims: God is present to place without being contained or defined by it.
God conserves place rather than being conserved by it.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e296.summary: The Damascene objection is answered in the same way as Anselm's.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e301.summary: Reply to the third objection: that a cause acting in absence and presence is nobler holds only of created causes with limited essence.
claims: The principle of nobility through action at a distance applies only to limited created causes.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e308.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: it is false that created causes give their effects power to persist if this excludes God's sustaining of creatures. So God is in every place by essence, presence and power, is neither circumscribed nor defined by any place, and is not 'local', and no separate questions on this are needed.
claims: No creature persists without God's sustaining action.
God is in every place by essence, presence and power without circumscription or definition.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e329.summary: First argument that God is equally in all things: the Liber de causis (prop. 24) says the first cause exists in all things in one disposition, even though things are not in it in one way.
claims: The first cause is in all things according to one disposition (argument).

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e347.summary: Second argument: the commentator on the Liber de causis says the one influencer pours goodness equally on all things; the diversity comes from the recipients.
claims: Diversity of reception comes from the recipients, not the first cause (argument).

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e358.summary: Third argument: God is supremely intimate to every creature, so he is not more intimate to one than another.
claims: God is equally and supremely intimate to every creature (argument).

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e363.summary: Sed contra from Gregory (gloss on Song of Songs 5, cited by Lombard): God is said to be more familiarly present by grace in those who consider his works more acutely and faithfully.
claims: God is present more familiarly by grace in some.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e375.summary: Second sed contra from Augustine to Dardanus: some saints are higher than others because they have God as indweller more abundantly.
claims: Saints differ by how abundantly God indwells them.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e384.summary: Richard's solution: by the common mode (essence, presence, power) God is equally in all things, being supremely intimate to all, beholding all with one intuition, and sustaining all equally. In vile things, such as the devil or hell, one should add 'insofar as they are creatures'. By influence, however, God is unequally present: more specially in those he influences by grace than by nature alone, so more in the saints, and most specially in Christ's human nature through fullness of grace and hypostatic union.
claims: By essence, presence and power God is equally in all things.
By influence God is unequally present: more by grace than by nature.
God is most specially present in Christ's humanity by hypostatic union.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e419.summary: The arguments for equality hold for God's common presence by essence, presence and power.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e426.summary: The arguments for inequality hold for God's presence by influence.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e436.summary: First objection against ubiquity being proper to God: place does not exist without body, nor body without matter, so matter is everywhere.
claims: Matter is everywhere (objection).

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e445.summary: Second objection: since the soul is whole in every part of its body, if only one human existed, the soul would be everywhere.
claims: A soul could be everywhere if its body were the only body (objection).

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e454.summary: Third objection: created being is everywhere but is not God.
claims: Created being is everywhere (objection).

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e459.summary: Fourth objection: Aristotle says the universal is everywhere and always, and the universal is not God.
claims: The universal is everywhere and always (objection).

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e467.summary: Fifth objection: whatever belongs to God by reason of his essence belongs to him from eternity, but God was not everywhere from eternity since there was no place, so ubiquity does not belong to God at all.
claims: What belongs to God essentially belongs to him eternally (objection).

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e483.summary: Sed contra: being everywhere belongs to God by reason of immensity, and no creature is immense.
claims: Ubiquity follows from immensity, which no creature has.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e492.summary: Second sed contra: Ambrose, cited by Lombard, proves the Holy Spirit is not a creature because he is everywhere, so ubiquity is proper to God.
claims: Ubiquity proves divinity.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e499.summary: Richard's solution: being everywhere per se and primo is proper to God alone. Per se means everywhere whatever the size or number of places, even infinite space; primo means everywhere as a whole, not by reason of parts. A creature can be everywhere only per accidens, given some hypothesis about the paucity of places (the soul if its body were the only body), or consequentially, by reason of its parts or singulars (matter, the universal, created being).
claims: To be everywhere per se and primo is proper to God alone.
Creatures can be everywhere only per accidens or by reason of their parts or instances.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e536.summary: The first four objections are resolved by the distinction just drawn.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e541.summary: Reply to the fifth objection: what belongs to God by essence belongs eternally only if it connotes nothing actual in creatures. As 'Lord' connotes servitude in creatures and so is not eternal, ubiquity connotes a real relation of all places to God, not of God to places, and there were no places from eternity. The sed contra arguments are true of ubiquity per se and primo.
claims: Predicates connoting something in creatures can be newly true of God.
Ubiquity implies a real relation of places to God, not of God to places.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e568.summary: First argument that God is outside every place: the Church sings that the one whom the whole world cannot contain enclosed himself in the Virgin's womb; what all places do not contain is outside every place.
claims: God exceeds the containment of the whole world (argument).

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e584.summary: Second argument: the Book of the XXIV Philosophers / Regulae theologiae (prop. 7) calls God an intelligible sphere whose center is everywhere and circumference nowhere, the center meaning creatures and the circumference divine immensity; so divine immensity is outside the world.
claims: Divine immensity extends beyond the world (argument).

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e597.summary: Third argument: Aristotle (De caelo I) says beyond heaven there is no place, void or time, yet there is fixed, everlasting life; so God is beyond the world.
claims: Aristotle places everlasting life beyond the heavens (argument).

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e610.summary: Sed contra: outside the world there is nothing, and God is not in nothing.
claims: Nothing exists outside the world.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e618.summary: Second sed contra: God is in nothing that is not in him, and nothing outside the world is in him.
claims: God is only in what is in him.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e625.summary: Richard's solution, first sense: God is outside the world in that his immensity exceeds, does not depend on, and is not defined by the world, as the infinite exceeds the finite (Bernard, Gregory). If a new world were created, God would be there not by moving but by his immensity, which exceeds this world's capacity infinitely.
claims: God's immensity infinitely exceeds the world and is not bounded by it.
God would be present in any newly created world without change.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e654.summary: Second sense, rejected: God is not outside the world in the sense that there is some real space beyond the world in which God exists; that would confirm the false opinion of infinite space beyond the last heaven. This largely resolves the arguments on both sides.
claims: There is no real space beyond the outermost heaven.
The opinion of infinite extramundane space is false.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e672.summary: The first two arguments for God's being outside the world hold in the first, true sense.

kzz7yh-a78315-d1e679.summary: Reply to the Aristotle argument: it can be read in the first sense, or Aristotle may have meant that life is in the last heaven ('illic' referring to it); if he meant God is beyond the heaven, he spoke correctly in the conceded sense. The sed contra arguments are true against positing extramundane space.
claims: Aristotle's 'life beyond heaven' is acceptable if read as divine transcendence, not spatial location.

kzz7yh-a78315-Dd1e126.summary: Question 1 holds that God is in all things by essence, presence and power. By essence because of his positive infinity and simplicity, so that he is whole in each, and because creatures emanate from him immediately and his essence is identical with his power. By presence because all things lie open to his knowledge. By power because creatures always need to be conserved. These modes refute those who limit the divine essence, those who deny providence, and the Manichees. The replies interpret Anselm and the Damascene as denying only that God is contained in place, restrict action at a distance to limited causes, and reject any creaturely independence from conservation.
claims: God is in all things by essence, presence and power.
God is present to place without being circumscribed or defined.
Creatures require continual divine conservation.

kzz7yh-a78315-Dd1e325.summary: Question 2 resolves whether God is equally in all things by distinguishing two modes of presence. In the common mode (essence, presence, power) God is equally in all, being supremely intimate, all-seeing and sustaining, with the caveat that he is in vile things only insofar as they are creatures. By influence he is unequally present: more by grace than by nature, so more in the saints, and supremely in Christ's humanity through grace and union. Both sets of arguments are true under their respective modes.
claims: God's common presence is equal in all things.
God's presence by influence of grace is unequal, highest in Christ's humanity.

kzz7yh-a78315-Dd1e432.summary: Question 3 holds that being everywhere per se and primo, that is, under any hypothesis about the extent of space and as a whole rather than through parts, belongs to God alone and follows from his immensity. Creatures can be everywhere only per accidens (the soul under a hypothesis) or consequentially through their parts or instances (matter, universals, created being). Against the objection from eternity, ubiquity is a temporal predicate connoting a real relation of places to God, like 'Lord', so it begins with the creation of places.
claims: Ubiquity per se and primo is proper to God.
Creatures are everywhere only per accidens or through their parts.
Ubiquity is a temporal predicate implying a real relation of creatures to God only.

kzz7yh-a78315-Dd1e564.summary: Question 4 asks whether God is outside every place and distinguishes two senses. In the true sense, God's immensity infinitely exceeds the world, does not depend on it and is not bounded by it, so he would be present in a newly created world without moving. In the false sense, God exists in some real space beyond the world; Richard rejects this together with the opinion of infinite extramundane space. The Marian antiphon, the infinite sphere image and Aristotle's De caelo are read in the first sense.
claims: God's immensity exceeds the world without implying extramundane space.
There is no real space beyond the last heaven.

kzz7yh-a78315.summary: Article 1 of Book I d.37 treats God's existence in things in four questions. God is in all things by essence (from immensity, simplicity and immediate causation), by presence (omniscience) and by power (continual conservation). In this common mode he is equally in all things, but by influence of grace he is unequally present, supremely in Christ's humanity. Being everywhere per se and primo is proper to God because of his immensity; creatures are everywhere only per accidens or through their parts, and ubiquity is a temporal predicate implying a real relation of places to God. God is 'outside the world' in that his immensity exceeds it, but not as though there were real space beyond the heavens.
claims: God is in all things by essence, presence and power.
God's common presence is equal in all; his presence by grace is unequal.
Ubiquity per se and primo belongs to God alone.
God's immensity exceeds the world without any extramundane space.
